regiones/caucaso/resumen.texto: The isthmus between the Black Sea and the Caspian, with the Greater Caucasus range: Georgia, Azerbaijan and the Russian republics of the north, such as Dagestan and Chechnya (Armenia has its own region). It was a frontier between Rome and Persia, and of Byzantines, Arabs, Ottomans and Safavids, and Russia conquered it in the 19th century after a long war with the mountain peoples.

regiones/caucaso/eras.0.nombre.texto: Colchis and the peoples of the Caucasus

regiones/caucaso/eras.6.nombre.texto: Georgia, Azerbaijan and the Russian Caucasus

regiones/caucaso/eras.0.resumen.texto: Colchis, on the Black Sea coast, is the land of the Golden Fleece of Greek myth; the Greeks found colonies on its coast.

regiones/caucaso/eras.1.resumen.texto: Kingdoms between Rome and Persia; Iberia (Kartli) adopts Christianity c. 330, and Caucasian Albania, to the east, is also Christianized.

regiones/caucaso/eras.2.resumen.texto: The caliphate rules Tiflis and Caucasian Albania, which is Islamized; Derbent is its fortress against the Khazars.

regiones/caucaso/eras.3.resumen.texto: Bagrat III unites Georgia in 1008; under David IV and Queen Tamar it enjoys its golden age, while the Shirvanshahs rule the east.

regiones/caucaso/eras.4.resumen.texto: After the Mongols and Tamerlane, the Caucasus is divided between the Ottomans and Safavid Persia; Georgia splits into lesser kingdoms.

regiones/caucaso/eras.5.resumen.texto: Russia annexes eastern Georgia in 1801, conquers the rest in wars with Persia and Turkey, and subdues the mountain peoples in the Caucasian War (1817-1864).

regiones/caucaso/eras.6.resumen.texto: Independence of Georgia and Azerbaijan; wars in Chechnya (1994-2009), Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

regiones/caucaso/demografia.0.nota.texto: Georgia and Azerbaijan; the North Caucasus is counted with Russia (Rus region), and Armenia has its own series.

regiones/norte-ruso/resumen.texto: The northern lands of European Russia, from the Kola Peninsula and Karelia to the White Sea and the Komi Republic: taiga and tundra inhabited by Uralic peoples such as the Sami, Karelians, Komi and Nenets. Novgorod explored them from the 11th century in search of furs, and Arkhangelsk was Russia's great port to Europe until the founding of Saint Petersburg.

regiones/norte-ruso/eras.0.resumen.texto: The Sami, Karelians, Veps, Komi and Nenets live by hunting, fishing and reindeer herding.

regiones/norte-ruso/eras.1.resumen.texto: Novgorod levies tribute in furs and founds outposts on the Dvina; Stephen of Perm evangelizes the Komi in the 14th century.

regiones/norte-ruso/eras.2.resumen.texto: Moscow inherits the north; Arkhangelsk (1584) is the port for trade with England and Holland, and the Solovetsky Monastery a great religious center.

regiones/norte-ruso/eras.3.resumen.texto: Saint Petersburg displaces Arkhangelsk; the north remains a land of timber, fishing and exile.

regiones/norte-ruso/eras.4.resumen.texto: Murmansk becomes a naval base and Arctic port; Gulag camps operate in Komi and Vorkuta.

regiones/volga-urales/resumen.texto: The middle course of the Volga and the Kama up to the Ural Mountains, with Kazan, Samara, Ufa and Perm. It was the land of Volga Bulgaria, which adopted Islam in 922, and of the Khanate of Kazan, until Ivan the Terrible conquered it in 1552; today Russians, Tatars, Bashkirs, Chuvash, Mari and Udmurts live side by side there.

regiones/volga-urales/eras.0.resumen.texto: Ancestors of the Mari, Udmurts and Mordvins in the forests; nomads in the southern steppe.

regiones/volga-urales/eras.1.resumen.texto: State of the Volga Bulgars, hub of the fur trade between the Baltic and the caliphate; adopts Islam in 922.

regiones/volga-urales/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Mongols destroy Bulgar in 1236 and the region falls within the Golden Horde.

regiones/volga-urales/eras.3.resumen.texto: Tatar khanate that emerged from the Golden Horde, rival of Moscow.

regiones/volga-urales/eras.4.resumen.texto: Russian conquest of Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan (1556), Russian colonization, Pugachev's Rebellion (1773-1775) and mining in the Urals.

regiones/volga-urales/eras.5.resumen.texto: Autonomous republics of Tatarstan, Bashkortostan, Chuvashia and others; in the Second World War it receives evacuated industry.

regiones/siberia/resumen.texto: The plains and plateaus between the Urals and Lake Baikal, watered by the Ob, the Irtysh and the Yenisei. Inhabited by Samoyedic, Ugric, Turkic and Tungusic peoples, it passed from the Khanate of Sibir to Russia with the expedition of the Cossack Yermak (1582) and was a land of furs, of exile and, in the 20th century, of the Gulag and heavy industry.

regiones/siberia/eras.0.nombre.texto: Peoples of the taiga and the steppe

regiones/siberia/eras.1.nombre.texto: Mongols and the Khanate of Sibir

regiones/siberia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Hunters, fishers and reindeer herders; in the south, steppe cultures such as Pazyryk (Altai) and the Yenisei Kyrgyz.

regiones/siberia/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Mongols subdue the forest peoples in 1207; later the Tatar Khanate of Sibir dominates the Irtysh.

regiones/siberia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Yermak takes Isker in 1582 and the Cossacks reach the Pacific within half a century; the Trans-Siberian Railway is built between 1891 and 1916.

regiones/siberia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Gulag camps, industrialization, cities such as Novosibirsk and the exploitation of oil and gas.

regiones/lejano-oriente-ruso/resumen.texto: Eastern Siberia and the Pacific coast: Yakutia, the Amur, Kamchatka, Chukotka and Sakhalin. A land of Yakuts, Evenks, Chukchi and other peoples; Russian Cossacks reached the Sea of Okhotsk in 1639 and China ceded the Amur to Russia in 1858-1860, when Vladivostok was founded. The tip of Chukotka, east of the 180th meridian, lies outside the polygon.

regiones/lejano-oriente-ruso/eras.0.resu.texto: Yakuts, Evenks, Chukchi, Itelmens and Nivkhs; on the Amur, kingdoms such as Balhae and the Jurchens.

regiones/lejano-oriente-ruso/eras.1.resu.texto: Founding of Yakutsk (1632) and Okhotsk (1647); Russia and Qing China set the border at Nerchinsk (1689) and Bering explores the strait that bears his name.

regiones/lejano-oriente-ruso/eras.2.resu.texto: Russia obtains the Amur and the Ussuri (1858-1860), founds Vladivostok and loses the war with Japan (1904-1905), which takes southern Sakhalin.

regiones/lejano-oriente-ruso/eras.3.resu.texto: Civil war and Japanese intervention (1918-1922), Gulag camps in Kolyma and recovery of southern Sakhalin and the Kuril Islands in 1945.

regiones/tibet/resumen.texto: The highest plateau in the world, between the Himalayas and the Kunlun, with Lhasa, Amdo and Kham. The Tibetan Empire (7th to 9th centuries) rivaled the Tang; since then Tibetan Buddhism and its monasteries have shaped the region, governed from 1642 by the Dalai Lamas until China occupied it in 1950-1951. The polygon includes Bhutan, northern Nepal and Ladakh.

regiones/tibet/eras.0.nombre.texto: Zhangzhung and peoples of the plateau

regiones/tibet/eras.2.nombre.texto: Fragmentation and the second diffusion of Buddhism

regiones/tibet/eras.0.resumen.texto: Kingdom of Zhangzhung in the west and the Bön religion.

regiones/tibet/eras.1.resumen.texto: Songtsen Gampo unifies the plateau; the empire occupies Chang'an in 763 and adopts Buddhism.

regiones/tibet/eras.2.resumen.texto: After the fall of the empire, Buddhist schools such as the Kagyu and the Sakya emerge.

regiones/tibet/eras.3.resumen.texto: The Mongols delegate government to the Sakya lamas; later the Phagmodrupa and the Tsangpa rule.

regiones/tibet/eras.4.resumen.texto: The Fifth Dalai Lama rules with Mongol support; the Qing exercise a protectorate from 1720 and Tibet declares independence in 1913.

regiones/tibet/eras.5.resumen.texto: Chinese occupation (1950-1951), the 1959 uprising and the Dalai Lama's exile in India; autonomous region since 1965.

regiones/turquestan-oriental/resumen.texto: The Tarim Basin, with the Taklamakan Desert ringed by oases such as Kashgar, Khotan and Turpan, and Dzungaria to the north. The central stretch of the Silk Road, it was a land of Tocharian and Saka kingdoms, of Buddhist monasteries and of the Uyghur kingdom of Qocho, and came under China with the Qing in 1759. The polygon includes the Hexi Corridor.

regiones/turquestan-oriental/eras.0.resu.texto: Tocharian and Saka city-states (Kucha, Turpan, Khotan), contested by the Han, the Xiongnu, the Tang and Tibet; center of Silk Road Buddhism.

regiones/turquestan-oriental/eras.1.resu.texto: After the fall of the Uyghur Khaganate (840), the Uyghurs found the kingdom of Qocho in Turpan; in the west, the Karakhanids adopt Islam and conquer Khotan c. 1006.

regiones/turquestan-oriental/eras.2.resu.texto: Chagatai Khanate and later the Yarkand Khanate (1514-1705); the region becomes Islamized.

regiones/turquestan-oriental/eras.3.resu.texto: The Dzungars dominate the region until the Qing destroy them (1755-1759).

regiones/turquestan-oriental/eras.4.resu.texto: The Qing call it Xinjiang (new frontier) and make it a province in 1884; there were East Turkestan republics in 1933-1934 and 1944-1949.

regiones/turquestan-oriental/eras.5.resu.texto: Uyghur autonomous region since 1955; since 2017, mass detention of Uyghurs in camps, which a 2022 UN report considered possible crimes against humanity.

regiones/asia-central/resumen.texto: The steppes of Kazakhstan and the oases of Transoxiana, between the Caspian and the Tian Shan: Samarkand, Bukhara, Khiva and the Fergana Valley. A crossroads of the Silk Road, it was a land of Sakas, Sogdians and Turkic peoples, a center of Islamic science with al-Khwarizmi, al-Biruni and Avicenna, and the capital of Tamerlane's empire.

regiones/asia-central/eras.0.resumen.texto: Scythians (Sakas) on the steppe; in the oases, Bactria, Sogdiana and Chorasmia pay tribute to the Achaemenid Empire.

regiones/asia-central/eras.1.resumen.texto: Alexander reaches Maracanda (Samarkand); there follow the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, the Kushans, the Hephthalites and the Turkic khaganates, while Sogdian merchants dominate the Silk Road.

regiones/asia-central/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Arabs conquer Transoxiana (Battle of Talas, 751); under the Samanids, Karakhanids and Khwarazmians, Bukhara and Samarkand flourish.

regiones/asia-central/eras.3.resumen.texto: Genghis Khan devastates Khwarazm (1219-1221); the region falls to the Chagatai Khanate and, in the north, to the Golden Horde.

regiones/asia-central/eras.4.resumen.texto: Tamerlane and his successors make Samarkand and Herat capitals of the arts and sciences; Ulugh Beg builds his observatory.

regiones/asia-central/eras.5.resumen.texto: Bukhara, Khiva and Kokand in the oases; the Kazakh khanates on the steppe.

regiones/asia-central/eras.6.resumen.texto: Russia takes Tashkent in 1865 and subdues the khanates; the USSR creates the present-day republics and dries up the Aral Sea.

regiones/asia-central/eras.7.resumen.texto: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.

regiones/asia-central/demografia.0.nota.texto: Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.

regiones/afganistan/resumen.texto: The mountains of the Hindu Kush and the lands of Kabul, Herat, Kandahar and Balkh, between Persia, Central Asia and India. It was the Bactria and Arachosia of antiquity, part of the Buddhist world of Gandhara, with the Buddhas of Bamiyan, and the base of empires such as the Ghaznavid and the Durrani. The polygon includes Pakistani Balochistan.

regiones/afganistan/eras.0.resumen.texto: Bactria, Arachosia and Gandhara pay tribute to Persia.

regiones/afganistan/eras.1.resumen.texto: After Alexander, the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom and the Kushan Empire, with its Greco-Buddhist art.

regiones/afganistan/eras.2.resumen.texto: Sasanian Persia and the Hephthalites rule; the great Buddhas are carved at Bamiyan (6th century).

regiones/afganistan/eras.3.resumen.texto: Mahmud of Ghazni (998-1030) launches his campaigns into India; the Ghurids open the way to the Delhi Sultanate.

regiones/afganistan/eras.4.resumen.texto: Herat is the Timurid capital and Babur sets out from Kabul to conquer India (1526).

regiones/afganistan/eras.5.resumen.texto: Ahmad Shah Durrani founds the Afghan state in 1747; wars with Britain (1839-1842 and 1878-1880).

regiones/afganistan/eras.6.resumen.texto: Monarchy until 1973; Soviet invasion (1979-1989), civil war, Taliban regime and US occupation (2001-2021).

regiones/afganistan/demografia.0.nota.texto: Afghanistan; Pakistani Balochistan, within the polygon, is counted under India.

regiones/manchuria/resumen.texto: Northeast China, with the plains of the Liao, the Sungari and the Amur. A land of Tungusic peoples, it was the base of the kingdoms of Goguryeo and Balhae, of the Khitans, of the Jurchens of the Jin dynasty and of the Manchus, who conquered China in 1644 and founded the Qing dynasty.

regiones/manchuria/eras.0.resumen.texto: The Korean kingdom of Goguryeo dominates southern Manchuria and northern Korea.

regiones/manchuria/eras.1.resumen.texto: Kingdom founded by Dae Joyeong, heir of Goguryeo, with a Mohe population.

regiones/manchuria/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Khitans (Liao, 907-1125) and the Jurchens (Jin, 1115-1234) rule northern China from here.

regiones/manchuria/eras.3.resumen.texto: After the Mongols, the Ming control Liaodong; the Jurchen tribes live to the north.

regiones/manchuria/eras.4.resumen.texto: Nurhaci founds the Later Jin (1616); his son adopts the name Manchu and the Qing dynasty conquers China in 1644.

regiones/manchuria/eras.5.resumen.texto: Contested by Russia and Japan, which creates the puppet state of Manchukuo (1932-1945); today it forms China's northeastern provinces.

regiones/mongolia/resumen.texto: The steppe and the Gobi Desert between Siberia and China, including China's Inner Mongolia. Cradle of great nomadic confederations such as the Xiongnu, the Xianbei, the Rouran and the Turkic and Uyghur khaganates, it was from here that Genghis Khan created in 1206 the largest contiguous empire in history.

regiones/mongolia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Nomadic confederation unified by Modu Chanyu in 209 BC, rival of the Han.

regiones/mongolia/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Xianbei and later the Rouran Khaganate dominate the steppe.

regiones/mongolia/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Göktürks (552-744), with the Orkhon inscriptions, and the Uyghur Khaganate (744-840).

regiones/mongolia/eras.3.resumen.texto: The Khitan Liao dynasty (907-1125) dominates the east; Mongol, Tatar and Kereit tribes vie for the steppe.

regiones/mongolia/eras.4.resumen.texto: Genghis Khan is proclaimed in 1206; Karakorum is the capital until Kublai moves it to Beijing.

regiones/mongolia/eras.5.resumen.texto: After their expulsion from China, the Mongol khans split; Altan Khan adopts Tibetan Buddhism (1578).

regiones/mongolia/eras.6.resumen.texto: Outer Mongolia submits to the Qing in 1691.

regiones/mongolia/eras.7.resumen.texto: Outer Mongolia becomes independent (people's republic from 1924 to 1992); Inner Mongolia remains part of China.

regiones/mongolia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Mongolia; Inner Mongolia, within the polygon, is counted under China.

regiones/china-meridional/resumen.texto: Southern China: Guangdong, Fujian, Guangxi, Yunnan, Guizhou, Hainan, Hong Kong and Macau. Land of the Baiyue peoples, the kingdom of Nanyue and the kingdoms of Nanzhao and Dali, it was integrated into the Chinese world over two millennia and, through its ports, connected China with the trade of the Indian Ocean and Europe.

regiones/china-meridional/eras.0.resumen.texto: Peoples speaking Tai-Kadai, Austroasiatic and Hmong-Mien languages, with rice and bronze cultures.

regiones/china-meridional/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Qin conquer Lingnan; the kingdom of Nanyue (204-111 BC) rules it until the Han annex it.

regiones/china-meridional/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Han, the Southern dynasties and the Tang colonize the south; Guangzhou receives Arab and Persian merchants; in Yunnan, the kingdom of Nanzhao (738-902).

regiones/china-meridional/eras.3.resumen.texto: Under the Southern Song, maritime trade flourishes at Quanzhou and Guangzhou; the kingdom of Dali, in Yunnan, falls to the Mongols in 1253.

regiones/china-meridional/eras.4.resumen.texto: Zheng He sets sail from Fujian; the Portuguese settle in Macau (1557) and Guangzhou is the only port open to Europe (1757-1842).

regiones/china-meridional/eras.5.resumen.texto: Hong Kong passes to Britain (1842); the Taiping Rebellion begins in Guangxi and Sun Yat-sen leads the republican revolution from Guangzhou.

regiones/china-meridional/eras.6.resumen.texto: Shenzhen becomes the first special economic zone (1980); Hong Kong (1997) and Macau (1999) return to China.

regiones/taiwan/resumen.texto: The island of Formosa, inhabited by Austronesian peoples for some 6000 years and the probable starting point of the Austronesian expansion across the Pacific. It was a Dutch colony, the kingdom of Koxinga, part of the Qing Empire and a Japanese colony, and since 1949 it has been the seat of the government of the Republic of China.

regiones/taiwan/eras.0.resumen.texto: Indigenous peoples speaking Austronesian languages; from the 16th century, fishermen and pirates arrive from Fujian.

regiones/taiwan/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Dutch East India Company in the south and Spain in the north (1626-1642).

regiones/taiwan/eras.2.resumen.texto: Koxinga expels the Dutch and his heirs resist the Qing.

regiones/taiwan/eras.3.resumen.texto: Mass colonization from Fujian and Guangdong.

regiones/taiwan/eras.4.resumen.texto: Japanese colony after the Sino-Japanese War.

regiones/taiwan/eras.5.resumen.texto: The Kuomintang retreats to the island in 1949; martial law until 1987 and democracy since the 1990s.

regiones/corea/resumen.texto: The Korean Peninsula, between China, Manchuria and Japan. After the Three Kingdoms (Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla), it was unified by Silla, Goryeo and the Joseon dynasty, which created the Hangul alphabet in 1443; a Japanese colony between 1910 and 1945, it was left divided into two states after the 1950-1953 war.

regiones/corea/eras.0.resumen.texto: The first Korean state according to tradition; falls to the Han in 108 BC.

regiones/corea/eras.1.resumen.texto: Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla; Buddhism arrives from China.

regiones/corea/eras.2.resumen.texto: Silla unites the south with Tang help; in the north, Balhae.

regiones/corea/eras.3.resumen.texto: The dynasty that gives Korea its name; it prints with movable metal type (Jikji, 1377) and resists the Mongols.

regiones/corea/eras.4.resumen.texto: Confucian dynasty; Sejong creates Hangul (1443) and the country withstands the Japanese invasions of 1592-1598.

regiones/corea/eras.6.resumen.texto: Division in 1945, the Korean War (1950-1953) and two states to this day.

regiones/japon/resumen.texto: The archipelago of Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu and Shikoku (the Ryukyu Islands lie outside the polygon). After the Jōmon and Yayoi cultures, the Yamato state formed and adopted writing, Buddhism and institutions from China; the shoguns ruled from the late 12th century until 1868, and the Meiji Restoration turned the country into an industrial power.

regiones/japon/eras.6.nombre.texto: Meiji and the Empire of Japan

regiones/japon/eras.0.resumen.texto: Hunter-gatherers with one of the oldest pottery traditions in the world.

regiones/japon/eras.1.resumen.texto: Irrigated rice farming and metal arrive from the continent.

regiones/japon/eras.2.resumen.texto: Great burial mounds and the Yamato state; Buddhism arrives in the 6th century and Prince Shōtoku promotes reforms.

regiones/japon/eras.3.resumen.texto: Capitals at Nara and Kyoto; Murasaki Shikibu writes The Tale of Genji.

regiones/japon/eras.4.resumen.texto: Samurai rule; the Mongol invasions (1274 and 1281) fail and civil wars follow until unification.

regiones/japon/eras.5.resumen.texto: The Tokugawa shogunate closes the country and urban culture flourishes in Edo.

regiones/japon/eras.6.resumen.texto: Rapid modernization, colonial expansion and the Pacific War.

regiones/japon/eras.7.resumen.texto: US occupation, the 1947 constitution and strong economic growth.

regiones/sur-de-la-india/resumen.texto: The Deccan Plateau and the coasts of the southern subcontinent: Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Odisha. Land of the Dravidian languages and of Tamil Sangam poetry, it was the seat of empires such as the Satavahana, Chalukya, Chola and Vijayanagara, and its ports traded with Rome, Southeast Asia and the Arab world.

regiones/sur-de-la-india/eras.0.resumen.texto: Tamil Sangam poetry; the Satavahanas in the Deccan; trade with Rome through Muziris.

regiones/sur-de-la-india/eras.1.resumen.texto: Kingdoms that build the temples of Mahabalipuram and Badami.

regiones/sur-de-la-india/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Cholas dominate the south and launch naval expeditions as far as Sumatra (1025).

regiones/sur-de-la-india/eras.3.resumen.texto: The Hindu empire of Vijayanagara, with its capital at Hampi, against the Bahmani Sultanate and its successors, who defeat it at Talikota (1565).

regiones/sur-de-la-india/eras.4.resumen.texto: Shivaji founds Maratha power; the Mughals conquer the Deccan and the British East India Company establishes its dominance from Madras.

regiones/sur-de-la-india/eras.5.resumen.texto: The Madras and Bombay presidencies and princely states such as Hyderabad and Mysore; since 1947, India.

regiones/noreste-de-la-india/resumen.texto: The Brahmaputra Valley and the surrounding hills: Assam, Meghalaya, Manipur, Nagaland, Mizoram and Tripura, with part of Bangladesh. A land of Tibeto-Burman, Tai and Austroasiatic peoples, it was here that the Ahom kingdom ruled Assam for six centuries, until the Burmese invasion and the British conquest.

regiones/noreste-de-la-india/eras.0.resu.texto: The kingdom of Kamarupa in the Brahmaputra Valley.

regiones/noreste-de-la-india/eras.1.resu.texto: The Ahoms, of Tai origin, rule Assam and repel the Mughals at Saraighat (1671).

regiones/noreste-de-la-india/eras.2.resu.texto: After the war with Burma, the British annex Assam and establish the tea plantations.

regiones/noreste-de-la-india/eras.3.resu.texto: Indian states of the northeast, with long-running insurgent conflicts.

regiones/sri-lanka/resumen.texto: The island of Ceylon, off the southern tip of India. Its Pali chronicles, such as the Mahavamsa, tell a continuous history from the kingdoms of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa onward; it was a center of Theravada Buddhism and, from the 16th century, a Portuguese, Dutch and British colony, until its independence in 1948.

regiones/sri-lanka/eras.0.resumen.texto: Capital of Sinhalese kingdoms; Buddhism arrives in the 3rd century BC.

regiones/sri-lanka/eras.1.resumen.texto: After the Chola invasion the capital moves to Polonnaruwa; in the north, the Tamil kingdom of Jaffna arises.

regiones/sri-lanka/eras.2.resumen.texto: European powers control the coasts while the kingdom of Kandy holds out in the interior.

regiones/sri-lanka/eras.3.resumen.texto: Britain takes the island and conquers Kandy in 1815; coffee and tea plantations.

regiones/sri-lanka/eras.4.resumen.texto: Independence in 1948 and civil war between the state and the Tamil Tigers (1983-2009).

regiones/sudeste-asiatico/resumen.texto: The Indochinese Peninsula: Burma, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam, with the valleys of the Irrawaddy, the Chao Phraya and the Mekong. It received influences from India and China, and Funan, Angkor, Pagan, Ayutthaya and Đại Việt flourished there; Thailand was the only country in the region not colonized by Europeans.

regiones/sudeste-asiatico/eras.0.nombre.texto: Dong Son, Funan and Indianized kingdoms

regiones/sudeste-asiatico/eras.1.nombre.texto: Angkor, Pagan, Champa and Đại Việt

regiones/sudeste-asiatico/eras.0.resumen.texto: The Dong Son Bronze Age culture in Vietnam and the kingdom of Funan in the Mekong Delta.

regiones/sudeste-asiatico/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Khmer Empire builds Angkor (9th to 13th centuries); Pagan unifies Burma (1044) and Vietnam becomes independent from China in 938.

regiones/sudeste-asiatico/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Siamese kingdom of Ayutthaya (1351-1767), Lan Xang in Laos and the Toungoo dynasty in Burma.

regiones/sudeste-asiatico/eras.3.resumen.texto: The Chakri in Bangkok (1782), the Konbaung in Burma and the Nguyen in Vietnam (1802).

regiones/sudeste-asiatico/eras.4.resumen.texto: France builds French Indochina (1858-1907) and Britain annexes Burma (1824-1885); Siam remains independent.

regiones/sudeste-asiatico/eras.5.resumen.texto: The Indochina and Vietnam wars, the Khmer Rouge regime in Cambodia (1975-1979) and integration into ASEAN.

regiones/sudeste-asiatico/demografia.0.n.texto: Burma, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam.

regiones/insulindia/resumen.texto: The Malay Archipelago: Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, the Philippines and East Timor. Settled by Austronesian peoples, it was the land of Srivijaya, Majapahit and Malacca, gateways of the spice trade between the Indian Ocean and China; Islam arrived from the 13th century onward and, from the 16th, the Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch and British divided the islands among themselves.

regiones/insulindia/eras.1.nombre.texto: Srivijaya and the kingdoms of Java

regiones/insulindia/eras.2.nombre.texto: Majapahit and the rise of Islam

regiones/insulindia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Austronesian seafarers; kingdoms such as Kutai and Tarumanagara adopt the writing and religion of India.

regiones/insulindia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Srivijaya dominates the Strait of Malacca; in Java, Borobudur and Prambanan are built (8th and 9th centuries).

regiones/insulindia/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Javanese empire of Majapahit and the Sultanate of Malacca, which spreads Islam.

regiones/insulindia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Portugal takes Malacca (1511), Spain colonizes the Philippines (1565), the Dutch East India Company dominates Java and the Moluccas, and Britain dominates Malaysia and Singapore.

regiones/insulindia/eras.4.resumen.texto: Indonesia (1945-1949), the Philippines (1946), Malaysia (1957), Singapore (1965), Brunei (1984) and East Timor (2002).

regiones/insulindia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brunei, the Philippines and East Timor.

regiones/sahara/resumen.texto: The desert south of the Maghreb: southern Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya, with the Fezzan, the Hoggar and Western Sahara. It was green during the Holocene humid period, as the paintings of the Tassili show; later it was crossed by the caravans of the Garamantes and the Tuareg, which linked the Mediterranean with the Sahel.

regiones/sahara/eras.0.resumen.texto: Lakes and savannas; hunters and later herders leave the rock art of the Tassili and the Acacus.

regiones/sahara/eras.1.resumen.texto: Kingdom of the Fezzan with irrigation through underground galleries and trade with Carthage and Rome.

regiones/sahara/eras.2.resumen.texto: Islam and the trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt and slaves; the Tuareg in the Hoggar and the Aïr.

regiones/sahara/eras.3.resumen.texto: France, Italy and Spain divide up the desert; since independence, oil and gas in Algeria and Libya, and the Western Sahara conflict.

regiones/africa-occidental/resumen.texto: The Sahel and the Guinea coast, from the Senegal to Lake Chad: Senegal, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Ghana and their neighbors. There flourished the Nok culture, the Ghana, Mali and Songhai empires, the Hausa and Yoruba cities and the kingdoms of Benin and Ashanti; Timbuktu was a great center of Islamic learning, and from the 16th century the region suffered the Atlantic slave trade.

regiones/africa-occidental/eras.4.nombre.texto: Kingdoms and the Atlantic slave trade

regiones/africa-occidental/eras.0.resume.texto: The Nok culture, with its iron metallurgy and terracottas, and Djenné-Djenno on the middle Niger.

regiones/africa-occidental/eras.1.resume.texto: Wagadu controls the gold of the Sahel; Islam arrives with trans-Saharan merchants.

regiones/africa-occidental/eras.2.resume.texto: Sundiata Keita founds the empire; Mansa Musa makes his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 and Timbuktu becomes a center of learning.

regiones/africa-occidental/eras.3.resume.texto: Sonni Ali takes Timbuktu (1468); Morocco defeats the empire at Tondibi (1591).

regiones/africa-occidental/eras.4.resume.texto: Bornu, Oyo, Dahomey, Ashanti and the Sokoto Caliphate (1804); millions of people are taken to the Americas as slaves.

regiones/africa-occidental/eras.5.resume.texto: France and Great Britain divide up the region after the Berlin Conference.

regiones/africa-occidental/eras.6.resume.texto: Independence from Ghana (1957) onward; the Biafran War (1967-1970) and conflicts in the Sahel.

regiones/africa-occidental/demografia.0..texto: Sum of the sixteen West African countries, from Mauritania and Cape Verde to Nigeria and Niger.

regiones/sudan/resumen.texto: The plains of the Blue Nile and the White Nile south of Nubia, with Khartoum, Kordofan, Darfur and the Sudd. It was the land of the Christian kingdom of Alodia, the sultanates of Sennar and Darfur, the Mahdist State and the Anglo-Egyptian condominium; after independence (1956), long civil wars led to the secession of South Sudan in 2011. The Nubian Nile valley has its own region.

regiones/sudan/eras.0.resumen.texto: Christian kingdom with its capital at Soba, near present-day Khartoum.

regiones/sudan/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Funj found Sennar (1504) and the Darfur Sultanate dominates the west.

regiones/sudan/eras.2.resumen.texto: Muhammad Ali conquers Sudan; the slave trade from the south grows.

regiones/sudan/eras.3.resumen.texto: The Mahdi takes Khartoum (1885); the British defeat the Mahdist State at Omdurman (1898).

regiones/sudan/eras.4.resumen.texto: British rule jointly with Egypt; the south is administered separately.

regiones/sudan/eras.5.resumen.texto: Civil wars (1955-1972 and 1983-2005), the War in Darfur since 2003, independence of South Sudan (2011) and a new war since 2023.

regiones/sudan/demografia.0.nota.texto: Sudan and South Sudan, including Sudanese Nubia.

regiones/cuerno-de-africa/nombre.texto: Ethiopia and the Horn of Africa

regiones/cuerno-de-africa/resumen.texto: The highlands of Ethiopia and Eritrea and the coasts of Somalia and Djibouti. It was home to the Kingdom of Aksum, which adopted Christianity in the 4th century, and Christian Ethiopia kept its independence from European colonialism, except for the Italian occupation of 1936-1941; on the coast, Muslim cities traded with Arabia and India.

regiones/cuerno-de-africa/eras.0.resumen.texto: Highland kingdom with strong ties to southern Arabia.

regiones/cuerno-de-africa/eras.1.resumen.texto: Red Sea trading power that mints coins and adopts Christianity under Ezana, c. 330.

regiones/cuerno-de-africa/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Zagwe dynasty and the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela.

regiones/cuerno-de-africa/eras.3.resumen.texto: The Solomonic emperors against the Adal Sultanate, which under Ahmad Gragn nearly conquers Ethiopia (1529-1543); Gondar is the capital from 1636.

regiones/cuerno-de-africa/eras.4.resumen.texto: Tewodros II and Menelik II reunify the country; Ethiopia defeats Italy at Adwa (1896) and is occupied between 1936 and 1941.

regiones/cuerno-de-africa/eras.5.resumen.texto: Military rule of the Derg, independence of Eritrea (1993), collapse of the Somali state (1991) and the Tigray War (2020-2022).

regiones/africa-central/resumen.texto: The Congo Basin and the lands around it, from Lake Chad to Angola: Chad, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Gabon, the two Congos and Angola. From here the Bantu peoples spread; it was the land of the Kingdom of Kongo, the Luba and Lunda kingdoms and Kanem-Bornu, and it suffered the Atlantic slave trade and the regime of Leopold II's Congo Free State.

regiones/africa-central/eras.2.nombre.texto: Atlantic slave trade and inland kingdoms

regiones/africa-central/eras.0.resumen.texto: Bantu farmers spread from western Cameroon; in the north, Kanem is Islamized in the 11th century.

regiones/africa-central/eras.1.resumen.texto: The manikongo rules the mouth of the Congo; Afonso I (1509-1542) converts to Catholicism and writes to the king of Portugal against the slave trade.

regiones/africa-central/eras.2.resumen.texto: Portuguese Luanda, the Luba and Lunda kingdoms and Bornu on Lake Chad; millions of slaves leave for Brazil and the Caribbean.

regiones/africa-central/eras.3.resumen.texto: Leopold II's Congo Free State (1885-1908), with its atrocities against the population, and the French, Portuguese and Belgian colonies.

regiones/africa-central/eras.4.resumen.texto: Independence from 1960 onward (Angola in 1975), the Angolan Civil War (1975-2002) and the Congo Wars (1996-2003).

regiones/africa-central/demografia.0.not.texto: Chad, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon, the two Congos, Angola and São Tomé and Príncipe.

regiones/africa-oriental/nombre.texto: East Africa (Great Lakes and Swahili coast)

regiones/africa-oriental/resumen.texto: Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi: the Great Lakes region and the Indian Ocean coast. The Rift Valley and Olduvai hold some of the oldest human fossils; on the coast, Swahili cities such as Kilwa and Mombasa traded with Arabia, Persia and India, and inland, kingdoms such as Buganda and Rwanda arose.

regiones/africa-oriental/eras.2.nombre.texto: The Portuguese, Oman and the Great Lakes kingdoms

regiones/africa-oriental/eras.0.resumen.texto: Hunter-gatherers, Cushitic- and Nilotic-speaking herders and Bantu farmers.

regiones/africa-oriental/eras.1.resumen.texto: Kilwa, Mombasa, Zanzibar and Lamu, Muslim trading cities on the gold and ivory route.

regiones/africa-oriental/eras.2.resumen.texto: Vasco da Gama reaches Mombasa (1498); Oman dominates the coast and from 1840 rules from Zanzibar; inland, Buganda, Bunyoro and Rwanda.

regiones/africa-oriental/eras.3.resumen.texto: German and British East Africa; Rwanda and Burundi pass to Belgium in 1916.

regiones/africa-oriental/eras.4.resumen.texto: Independence (1961-1963) and the genocide of the Tutsi in Rwanda (1994).

regiones/africa-oriental/demografia.0.no.texto: Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda and Burundi.

regiones/africa-austral/resumen.texto: The south of the continent, from the Zambezi to the Cape of Good Hope: South Africa, Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Zambia, Malawi, Lesotho and Eswatini. Land of the San and Khoikhoi peoples and of Bantu farmers, it was the seat of Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe; from 1652 Dutch and later British settlers established themselves at the Cape, and South Africa lived under apartheid until 1994.

regiones/africa-austral/eras.1.nombre.texto: Bantu farmers, Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe

regiones/africa-austral/eras.3.nombre.texto: Colonization of the Cape and European expansion

regiones/africa-austral/eras.4.nombre.texto: Union of South Africa, apartheid and colonies

regiones/africa-austral/eras.0.resumen.texto: Hunter-gatherers and herders with a long tradition of rock art.

regiones/africa-austral/eras.1.resumen.texto: Kingdoms of gold and ivory: Mapungubwe (11th to 13th centuries) and Great Zimbabwe (13th to 15th centuries).

regiones/africa-austral/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Kingdom of Mutapa and the Portuguese in Sofala and on the Zambezi.

regiones/africa-austral/eras.3.resumen.texto: The Dutch East India Company founds Cape Town (1652); then come the Mfecane, the Zulu Kingdom, the Great Trek and the Anglo-Boer Wars.

regiones/africa-austral/eras.4.resumen.texto: Institutionalized racial segregation from 1948; the rest of the region becomes independent between 1964 and 1990.

regiones/africa-austral/eras.5.resumen.texto: Free elections and the presidency of Nelson Mandela.

regiones/africa-austral/demografia.0.not.texto: South Africa, Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Zambia, Malawi, Lesotho and Eswatini.

regiones/madagascar/nombre.texto: Madagascar and the Indian Ocean islands

regiones/madagascar/resumen.texto: Madagascar and the neighboring islands: the Comoros, Mauritius, Réunion, Mayotte and Seychelles (the most remote ones fall outside the polygon). Madagascar was settled by Austronesian seafarers from Borneo and by peoples from East Africa; the Merina kingdom unified much of the island in the 19th century, before French colonization (1896).

regiones/madagascar/eras.0.resumen.texto: Austronesian and Bantu seafarers arrive during the first millennium; Arabs trade on the coast.

regiones/madagascar/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Sakalava and Merina kingdoms; Andrianampoinimerina and Radama I unify the island from Antananarivo.

regiones/madagascar/eras.2.resumen.texto: French colony; the 1947 uprising is crushed, with tens of thousands killed.

regiones/madagascar/demografia.0.nota.texto: Madagascar, the Comoros, Mauritius, Seychelles, Réunion and Mayotte. There is no documented permanent settlement before AD 500: earlier values from the HYDE model are not shown.

regiones/norteamerica/resumen.texto: The United States and Canada, from the Arctic to the Gulf of Mexico (Hawaii and the most remote islands fall outside the polygon). Before European arrival it was inhabited by hundreds of Indigenous peoples, from the Mississippian mound cities such as Cahokia to the peoples of the Southwest and the Arctic; from the 17th century it was colonized by England, France and Spain, and in 1776 the United States was born.

regiones/norteamerica/eras.0.resumen.texto: Ice Age hunters and later cultures such as Adena and Hopewell.

regiones/norteamerica/eras.1.resumen.texto: Mound cities such as Cahokia (c. 1050-1350) and Chaco Canyon; the Norse in Newfoundland c. 1000 and Spanish and French explorations in the 16th century.

regiones/norteamerica/eras.2.resumen.texto: Jamestown (1607), Quebec (1608) and the Thirteen Colonies; France loses Canada in 1763.

regiones/norteamerica/eras.3.resumen.texto: Independence of the United States (1776), westward expansion at the expense of Indigenous peoples and the Civil War (1861-1865).

regiones/norteamerica/eras.4.resumen.texto: Canadian Confederation (1867); the United States becomes the world's largest economy.

regiones/norteamerica/demografia.0.nota.texto: The United States (including Alaska and Hawaii), Canada, Bermuda and Saint Pierre and Miquelon.

regiones/groenlandia/resumen.texto: The world's largest island, mostly covered by ice. Settled by successive Paleo-Eskimo cultures and by the Inuit of the Thule culture, it had Norse colonies from the late 10th century to the 15th century; Denmark and Norway colonized it again in 1721, and today it is an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark.

regiones/groenlandia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Erik the Red founds the Eastern and Western Settlements, which coexist with the Inuit of the Thule culture, who arrived around the 13th century, and disappear in the 15th century.

regiones/groenlandia/eras.2.resumen.texto: The Inuit are the island's only inhabitants.

regiones/groenlandia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Hans Egede's mission (1721) and colony of Denmark and Norway, later of Denmark.

regiones/aridoamerica/resumen.texto: Northern Mexico and the Baja California peninsula, north of Mesoamerica: deserts and mountain ranges inhabited by peoples such as the Rarámuri, Yaqui and Pima. Sites such as Paquimé traded with Mesoamerica and with the southwestern United States; the Spanish advanced in pursuit of the silver mines of Zacatecas from 1546.

regiones/aridoamerica/eras.0.resumen.texto: Hunter-gatherers and farmers; Paquimé (c. 1200-1450) is the great center of the northwest.

regiones/aridoamerica/eras.1.resumen.texto: Silver mines, the Chichimeca War (1550-1590) and the Jesuit missions of Sonora and the Californias.

regiones/aridoamerica/eras.2.resumen.texto: Mexico loses the north of its territory to the United States (1848) and the Porfiriato brings railways and haciendas.

regiones/aridoamerica/eras.3.resumen.texto: The Mexican Revolution breaks out in the north; industry and maquiladoras on the border.

regiones/caribe/resumen.texto: The Greater and Lesser Antilles and the Bahamas. Inhabited by the Taíno and Caribs, they were the first stage of the Spanish conquest (1492) and later of sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans; Haiti was the first independent country in Latin America (1804), after the only slave revolution that founded a state.

regiones/caribe/eras.0.resumen.texto: Arawakan (Taíno) and Carib peoples who came from South America.

regiones/caribe/eras.1.resumen.texto: Columbus arrives in 1492; the Taíno population collapses from violence and epidemics.

regiones/caribe/eras.2.resumen.texto: England, France and Holland divide up the Lesser Antilles, Jamaica and Saint-Domingue; massive slave trade.

regiones/caribe/eras.3.resumen.texto: Haiti (1804) and the Dominican Republic (1844); British (1834), French (1848) and Spanish (1873 in Puerto Rico and 1886 in Cuba) abolition.

regiones/caribe/eras.4.resumen.texto: Cuba independent after 1898, the Cuban Revolution (1959) and independence of the British colonies from 1962.

regiones/caribe/demografia.0.nota.texto: Sum of the countries and territories of the Antilles and the Bahamas. The islands were settled from c. 4000 BC: earlier values from the HYDE model are not shown.

regiones/centroamerica/resumen.texto: The isthmus south of Mesoamerica: Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama. Its Indigenous peoples, speaking Chibchan, Misumalpan and other languages, formed an intermediate area between Mesoamerica and the Andes; after the Spanish conquest it was part of the Captaincy General of Guatemala and the Viceroyalty of New Granada, and in 1914 the Panama Canal opened.

regiones/centroamerica/eras.0.resumen.texto: Agricultural chiefdoms, goldwork and the stone spheres of the Diquís, in Costa Rica.

regiones/centroamerica/eras.1.resumen.texto: Balboa crosses the isthmus and sights the Pacific (1513); Panama is the transit route for Peruvian silver.

regiones/centroamerica/eras.2.resumen.texto: Central American Federation (1823-1841); Panama remains part of Colombia until 1903.

regiones/centroamerica/eras.3.resumen.texto: Panama Canal (1914), Costa Rica without an army since 1948 and the Sandinista revolution in Nicaragua (1979).

regiones/centroamerica/demografia.0.nota.texto: Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica and Panama.

regiones/norte-de-sudamerica/resumen.texto: Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador and the Guianas, between the Caribbean, the northern Andes and the Amazon. Land of the Muisca, Tairona, Quitu and Cañari and of cultures such as Valdivia and San Agustín, it was the Viceroyalty of New Granada and the base of Bolívar, who formed Gran Colombia (1819-1831).

regiones/norte-de-sudamerica/eras.0.resu.texto: Valdivia, with one of the oldest pottery traditions in the Americas; San Agustín, the Muisca and the Tairona.

regiones/norte-de-sudamerica/eras.1.resu.texto: The Incas conquer the Ecuadorian highlands and Quito becomes the second capital of Tawantinsuyu.

regiones/norte-de-sudamerica/eras.2.resu.texto: Founding of Santa Marta (1525), Quito (1534) and Bogotá (1538); Viceroyalty of New Granada (1717) and British, Dutch and French colonies in the Guianas.

regiones/norte-de-sudamerica/eras.3.resu.texto: Bolívar liberates the region and forms Gran Colombia, which breaks up in 1831.

regiones/norte-de-sudamerica/eras.4.resu.texto: Colombia, Venezuela and Ecuador; Guyana (1966) and Suriname (1975) become independent and French Guiana remains part of France.

regiones/norte-de-sudamerica/demografia..texto: Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Guyana, Suriname and French Guiana.

regiones/brasil/resumen.texto: The largest country in South America, from the Amazon to the temperate south. Before 1500 it was inhabited by Tupi, Arawak and Gê peoples, with complex societies in the Amazon; it was a Portuguese colony from 1500, received about five million enslaved Africans and became independent in 1822 as an empire, before becoming a republic in 1889.

regiones/brasil/eras.0.resumen.texto: Tupi, Arawak and Gê societies; in the Amazon, chiefdoms such as Marajó (c. 400-1400).

regiones/brasil/eras.1.resumen.texto: Cabral arrives in 1500; the sugar of the northeast and the gold of Minas Gerais rely on slave labor.

regiones/brasil/eras.2.resumen.texto: Reigns of Pedro I and Pedro II; abolition of slavery in 1888.

regiones/brasil/eras.3.resumen.texto: Vargas Era, military dictatorship (1964-1985) and democracy.

regiones/gran-chaco/resumen.texto: The wooded plain between the Andes and the Paraguay and Paraná rivers: the Paraguayan and Bolivian Chaco and the west of the Argentine Chaco (the rest of the Argentine Chaco goes with the Río de la Plata). Inhabited by the Qom, Wichí, Mocoví and Chiriguanos, it resisted conquest until the late 19th century, and Bolivia and Paraguay fought over it in the Chaco War (1932-1935).

regiones/gran-chaco/eras.0.resumen.texto: Qom, Wichí, Mocoví, Chiriguanos and others, with Jesuit and Franciscan missions on the edges.

regiones/gran-chaco/eras.1.resumen.texto: Argentine military campaigns and the advance of the states into the Chaco.

regiones/gran-chaco/eras.2.resumen.texto: War between Bolivia and Paraguay, with some 90,000 dead.

regiones/gran-chaco/eras.3.resumen.texto: Quebracho logging, cattle ranching and Mennonite colonies in the Paraguayan Chaco.

regiones/gran-chaco/religiones.5.nombre.texto: Anglican and evangelical churches among Indigenous peoples

regiones/gran-chaco/religiones.5.nota.texto: The Anglican mission among the Wichí began in the early 1910s. From the mid-20th century, evangelical churches spread among the Qom.

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.0.nombre.texto: Peoples of the Gran Chaco (Guaycurú, Mataco-Mataguayan and others)

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.1.nombre.texto: Chiriguanos (Ava Guaraní) and Chanés of the foothills

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.2.nombre.texto: Spanish and criollos of forts, reductions and estancias on the edge of the Chaco

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.4.nombre.texto: Criollo, with European settlers (and Mennonites in the Paraguayan Chaco since 1927)

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.5.nombre.texto: Chaco peoples (Qom, Wichí, Pilagá, Mocoví, Nivaclé and others)

regiones/gran-chaco/culturas.0.nota.texto: There are few archaeological studies of the Chaco before the conquest. From the 17th century, the peoples of the south adopted the horse.

regiones/gran-chaco/idiomas.2.nombre.texto: Guaraní (Ava Guaraní; in the Paraguayan Chaco, also of the criollos)

regiones/gran-chaco/idiomas.0.nota.texto: The distribution of languages before the 16th century is not known.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/resumen.texto: The region east of the Paraguay River, except Asunción and its surroundings (which go with the Río de la Plata): a land of forests and rivers inhabited by the Guaraní, where the Jesuits organized their reductions in the 17th and 18th centuries. Today it is home to Ciudad del Este and the Itaipú Dam.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/eras.1.resume.texto: Asunción (1537) is the base of the Spanish colonization of the region.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/eras.2.resume.texto: The Jesuits found Guaraní towns, such as Trinidad and Jesús, until their expulsion.

regiones/paraguay-oriental/eras.3.resume.texto: Paraguay becomes independent in 1811 and is devastated by the War of the Triple Alliance (1864-1870).

regiones/paraguay-oriental/eras.4.resume.texto: Stroessner's dictatorship (1954-1989) and the Itaipú Dam (1984).

regiones/amazonia-andina/resumen.texto: The forests and plains of eastern Peru and Bolivia: Loreto, Ucayali, Madre de Dios, Beni, Pando and Santa Cruz. Inhabited by Amazonian peoples such as the Asháninka, Shipibo and Mojeño, who built earthworks and raised fields in the Llanos de Mojos, it was a mission frontier and, c. 1900, the scene of the rubber boom.

regiones/amazonia-andina/eras.0.resumen.texto: Societies of the forest and the Llanos de Mojos, with earthworks and raised fields.

regiones/amazonia-andina/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Jesuits found the missions of Mojos (1682) and Chiquitos.

regiones/amazonia-andina/eras.2.resumen.texto: After independence, Peru and Bolivia barely control the region.

regiones/amazonia-andina/eras.3.resumen.texto: Iquitos and Riberalta grow with rubber; abuses against Indigenous peoples, as in the Putumayo.

regiones/amazonia-andina/eras.4.resumen.texto: Colonization, oil, gas and agricultural expansion in Santa Cruz.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/resumen.texto: The valleys, puna and sierras of northwestern Argentina and the Cuyo region: Jujuy, Salta, Tucumán, Catamarca, La Rioja, San Juan, Mendoza and San Luis. Land of the Diaguita, Omaguaca, Atacama and Huarpe and of cultures such as La Aguada, it was the southeastern edge of Tawantinsuyu and the colonial route between Upper Peru and the Río de la Plata.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/eras.0.resum.texto: The Condorhuasi, Aguada and Santa María cultures; Diaguita, Omaguaca and Huarpe.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/eras.1.resum.texto: The Inca Empire incorporates the northwest and northern Cuyo into Collasuyu.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/eras.2.resum.texto: Founding of Santiago del Estero (1553), Mendoza (1561), Tucumán (1565), Salta (1582) and Jujuy (1593), and the Calchaquí Wars.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/eras.3.resum.texto: A front in the War of Independence (Güemes) and, later, Argentine provinces of sugar and wine.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/religiones.1.texto: Andean religion (hills, huacas and ancestors; Inca sun worship from the late 15th century)

regiones/noroeste-argentino/religiones.0.texto: Known only from rock art and burials.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/religiones.1.texto: Capacocha offerings on summits such as Llullaillaco show the religion of the Inca state.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/religiones.4.texto: Syncretic practices, strong in the puna and the valleys.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.0.n.texto: Hunter-gatherers of the puna and the valleys

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.1.n.texto: Andean farmers and herders of the Northwest (Tafí, Condorhuasi, Ciénaga, La Aguada, Santa María, Belén) and Huarpes in Cuyo

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.2.n.texto: Andean peoples under Inca rule (Diaguitas, Omaguacas, Atacamas, Huarpes)

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.3.n.texto: Diaguitas, Calchaquíes, Omaguacas, Atacamas and Huarpes, under encomienda or at war

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.4.n.texto: Spanish, criollos and mestizos of the cities (Tucumán, Mendoza, San Juan, Salta, La Rioja, Jujuy, Catamarca)

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.0.n.texto: Occupations such as that of Inca Cueva, about 10,000 years old. The domestication of the llama and the first crops led to herding and agriculture.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.2.n.texto: Chronicles date the Inca conquest to around 1471–1493; archaeological dates suggest it began a few decades earlier.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.3.n.texto: The Calchaquí valleys resisted until 1667; afterward many peoples were deported to other cities.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.5.n.texto: From 1880, with Spanish, Italian and Syrian-Lebanese immigration, mainly in Cuyo and Tucumán.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/culturas.6.n.texto: Predominant in the puna and the Quebrada de Humahuaca.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/idiomas.0.no.texto: Indigenous languages of the Northwest and Cuyo (Kakán, Kunza, Huarpe and others)

regiones/noroeste-argentino/idiomas.1.no.texto: Kakán, Kunza, Huarpe and other local languages

regiones/noroeste-argentino/idiomas.2.no.texto: Quechua, the general language of the Tawantinsuyu and of evangelization

regiones/noroeste-argentino/idiomas.0.no.texto: There is no record of the languages spoken before the conquest; those known were written down in the colonial period.

regiones/noroeste-argentino/idiomas.1.no.texto: Kakán died out toward the late 17th century without leaving texts. Of the Huarpe languages, there remain the works of Luis de Valdivia (1607).

regiones/patagonia/resumen.texto: The plateaus and the Patagonian Andes south of the Colorado River, down to Tierra del Fuego. Inhabited by the Tehuelche, Mapuche, Selk'nam and Yaghan, it was explored by Magellan in 1520 and occupied by the Argentine state in the so-called Conquest of the Desert (1878-1885). Chilean Patagonia goes with Chile, and the Falkland Islands (Malvinas) fall outside the polygon.

regiones/patagonia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Guanaco hunters and canoe peoples of the Fuegian channels; the paintings of the Cueva de las Manos are more than 9,000 years old.

regiones/patagonia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Magellan, Darwin and the Welsh of Chubut (1865); Patagonia remains in Indigenous hands.

regiones/patagonia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Conquest of the Desert, extermination of the Selk'nam, national territories and later provinces; oil in Comodoro Rivadavia (1907).

regiones/patagonia/religiones.0.nombre.texto: Religions of the Patagonian and Fuegian peoples

regiones/patagonia/religiones.4.nombre.texto: Protestantism (Welsh of Chubut, Anglican mission at Ushuaia)

regiones/patagonia/religiones.0.nota.texto: Among them, the initiation ceremonies of the selk'nam (Hain) and Yaghans that Gusinde recorded.

regiones/patagonia/culturas.0.nombre.texto: Nomadic hunters of Patagonia (ancestors of the Tehuelches and Gününa Küna; horse riders from the 18th century)

regiones/patagonia/culturas.2.nombre.texto: Mapuche of northern Patagonia (Pehuenches, País de las Manzanas)

regiones/patagonia/culturas.3.nombre.texto: Criollos of Carmen de Patagones and the coastal forts

regiones/patagonia/culturas.5.nombre.texto: Criollo, with Chilean and European immigrants

regiones/patagonia/culturas.0.nota.texto: Occupations dating back about 13,000 years at Piedra Museo and Los Toldos.

regiones/patagonia/culturas.1.nota.texto: Predominant in Tierra del Fuego until the massacres and epidemics of 1880–1920.

regiones/patagonia/culturas.2.nota.texto: The eastward spread of the Mapuche, called araucanización, is documented; its interpretation is debated.

regiones/patagonia/culturas.4.nota.texto: Welsh colony founded in 1865 in the lower valley of the Chubut River.

regiones/patagonia/idiomas.3.nombre.texto: Mapudungun, widely used in northern Patagonia

regiones/patagonia/idiomas.0.nota.texto: The languages of the first inhabitants are not known; the Chon languages are those recorded since the 16th century.

regiones/patagonia/idiomas.3.nota.texto: Its spread among the peoples of northern Patagonia is part of the so-called araucanización.

regiones/chile/resumen.texto: The long strip between the Andes and the Pacific, from the Atacama Desert to Tierra del Fuego. Inhabited by the Chinchorro, Atacameño, Diaguita, Mapuche and the peoples of the channels, its north was part of Tawantinsuyu; the Mapuche halted the Spanish conquest at the Biobío and kept Araucanía independent until the Chilean occupation of 1861-1883, and Chile became independent in 1818.

regiones/chile/eras.0.resumen.texto: The Chinchorro culture mummifies its dead from c. 5000 BC; Atacameño, Diaguita and Mapuche.

regiones/chile/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Incas reach the Maule River.

regiones/chile/eras.2.resumen.texto: Valdivia founds Santiago (1541); the Arauco War halts the Spanish at the Biobío.

regiones/chile/eras.3.resumen.texto: Independence (1818), the War of the Pacific against Peru and Bolivia (1879-1883) and the occupation of Araucanía.

regiones/chile/eras.4.resumen.texto: Saltpeter and copper; Pinochet's dictatorship (1973-1990) and democracy.

regiones/australia/resumen.texto: The Australian continent and Tasmania. Aboriginal peoples have lived there for at least 50,000 years, with one of the oldest continuous cultural traditions in the world; Great Britain founded a penal colony in Sydney in 1788, and in 1901 the colonies federated into the Commonwealth of Australia.

regiones/australia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Hundreds of peoples and languages, with rock art and millennia-old oral traditions; contacts with Macassan fishermen in the north.

regiones/australia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Penal and free colonies, the gold rush (1851) and the dispossession and massacres of Aboriginal peoples.

regiones/australia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Federation in 1901; the 1967 referendum includes Aboriginal people in the national census.

regiones/nueva-zelanda/resumen.texto: The North and South Islands, one of the last great landmasses settled by humans: the Polynesian ancestors of the Māori arrived c. 1250–1300. After the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) it was a British colony, and in 1907 it became a self-governing dominion; in 1893 it was the first country to give women the vote.

regiones/nueva-zelanda/eras.0.resumen.texto: Polynesians arrive c. 1250–1300 and develop Māori culture.

regiones/nueva-zelanda/eras.1.resumen.texto: Cook charts the islands; whalers and missionaries arrive, and the Musket Wars break out.

regiones/nueva-zelanda/eras.2.resumen.texto: Treaty of Waitangi (1840) and the New Zealand Wars over Māori land.

regiones/nueva-zelanda/eras.3.resumen.texto: Dominion from 1907 and fully sovereign from 1947.

regiones/nueva-zelanda/demografia.0.nota.texto: New Zealand. Polynesians arrived c. 1250–1300: earlier values from the HYDE model are not shown.

regiones/melanesia/resumen.texto: Eastern New Guinea (Papua New Guinea), the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji (the Indonesian half of New Guinea belongs to Maritime Southeast Asia). Agriculture was invented independently in the New Guinea Highlands between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago, and from about 3,000 years ago the seafarers of the Lapita culture spread through these islands on their way to Polynesia.

regiones/melanesia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Settlers who arrived more than 40,000 years ago; early agriculture at Kuk.

regiones/melanesia/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Lapita culture (c. 1600–500 BC) brings pottery and open-ocean navigation to the islands.

regiones/melanesia/eras.2.resumen.texto: European explorers from the 16th century; British, German, French and Australian colonies, and forced recruitment of laborers for Queensland and Fiji.

regiones/melanesia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Fiji (1970), Papua New Guinea (1975), the Solomon Islands (1978) and Vanuatu (1980); New Caledonia remains French.

regiones/melanesia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji.

regiones/micronesia/resumen.texto: Thousands of small islands and atolls north of Melanesia: Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia, the Marianas, the Marshall Islands, Nauru and Kiribati. The Marianas were settled by Austronesian seafarers about 3,500 years ago; the islands were a stopover for the Spanish galleons, a German and Japanese colony, and the scene of battles and nuclear tests in the 20th century.

regiones/micronesia/eras.0.resumen.texto: Settlement of the Marianas (c. 1500 BC) and then the rest; Nan Madol, on Pohnpei, is the capital of the Saudeleur.

regiones/micronesia/eras.1.resumen.texto: Magellan reaches Guam (1521), and Spain colonizes the Marianas from 1668.

regiones/micronesia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Germany buys the islands from Spain (1899) and Japan occupies them from 1914; battles of the Second World War.

regiones/micronesia/eras.3.resumen.texto: UN trust territory under the United States, nuclear tests at Bikini and Enewetak (1946–1958), and independence beginning with Nauru (1968).

regiones/micronesia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Federated States of Micronesia, Palau, Guam, Northern Mariana Islands, Marshall Islands, Nauru and Kiribati.

regiones/polinesia/resumen.texto: The great triangle of islands of the central and eastern Pacific: Samoa, Tonga, the Cook Islands, French Polynesia, Wallis and Futuna, Niue, Tokelau and Pitcairn. Its navigators, guided by the stars, the swells and the birds, settled these islands between c. 900 BC and 1300; Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island, also Polynesian, lie outside this polygon.

regiones/polinesia/eras.0.resumen.texto: From Tonga and Samoa the Polynesians reach the Society Islands and the Marquesas, and from there Hawaii, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa.

regiones/polinesia/eras.1.resumen.texto: The Tongan empire, the marae of Tahiti and societies of hereditary chiefs.

regiones/polinesia/eras.2.resumen.texto: Wallis reaches Tahiti (1767); Cook, the mutiny on the Bounty (1789) and the missionaries; France annexes Tahiti (1880).

regiones/polinesia/eras.3.resumen.texto: Samoa (1962) and Tonga (1970) become independent; France conducts nuclear tests at Mururoa (1966–1996).

regiones/polinesia/demografia.0.nota.texto: Samoa, American Samoa, Tonga, Niue, Wallis and Futuna, Tokelau, Cook Islands, French Polynesia and Tuvalu.
